content.title: About
content.content: Plain rice crispy cereal is a dry grain product made from whole rice that is toasted to a crisp texture. It contains no added sugar, flavorings, or colorings, making it a neutral base for breakfasts and snacks.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The flakes are produced from whole rice that is first cooked and then rapidly toasted in hot air.
Rice crisps are often used in gluten‑free diets because rice naturally lacks gluten.
Compared with corn flakes, rice crisps have a milder taste and absorb milk or yogurt more readily.
In the United States they are known as “Rice Krispies” and are a popular ingredient for desserts such as Rice Krispie Treats.
The flakes retain many B‑vitamins that are present in whole rice.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Rice crisps contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: The carbs are released slowly, providing sustained energy and a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Safe for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3 and B6 support energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Low fiber content makes them gentle on the stomach, useful during digestive upset.

items.title: Low protein and fiber
items.content: Rice crisps alone do not provide sufficient protein or dietary fiber, so they should be combined with other foods.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: They can raise blood sugar quickly, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes.

items.title: Rice allergy
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to rice.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour milk, yogurt, or a plant‑based drink over the flakes and add fresh berries, nuts, or dried fruit. They are also used in dessert recipes, snack bars, and as a crunchy coating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. For extended storage, refrigerate to prevent moisture absorption.

content.title: About
content.content: Clams are marine bivalve mollusks that are often prepared by baking or broiling. They have a delicate, slightly sweet flavor and a tender yet firm texture. Clams are eaten fresh, as well as canned or incorporated into prepared dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Clams filter water, helping to clean their environment.
In the wild, clams can live for more than 20 years.
They are an important source of protein in many coastal communities worldwide.
Clams feature in diverse cuisines, from French "clams in white wine" to Asian dishes with soy sauce.
There are over 1,000 clam species, but only a few commercial varieties dominate the market.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Clams provide about 10–12 g of protein per 100 g, making them a good source of high‑quality protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: They contain very little saturated fat and have lower calories than most meat products.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for blood formation and nervous system health; clams are one of the best natural sources.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals support immune function and various metabolic processes.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Clams provide modest amounts of EPA and DHA, beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to clams, ranging from mild symptoms to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Contamination risk
items.content: Clams can accumulate toxins and heavy metals from polluted waters; purchase from reputable sources.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Elevated purines may exacerbate gout symptoms in susceptible people.

items.title: Need for proper cooking
items.content: Raw clams may harbor pathogenic bacteria; they should be cooked until shells fully open.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Clams can be baked in the oven with herbs, garlic, and lemon or quickly broiled on a grill pan with butter. They are commonly served in sauces, soups, pastas, and salads. Before cooking, rinse thoroughly and remove the “beard” – the fibrous thread that protrudes from the shell.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh clams should be kept in the refrigerator in a tightly sealed container covered with a damp cloth, and used within 1–2 days. Frozen clams store best at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Discard any clams with open or cracked shells before cooking.

egg-omelet-or-scrambled-egg-with-cheese-.title: Egg omelet with cheese and meat, cooked in animal fat

content.title: About
content.content: An egg omelet with cheese and meat, cooked in animal fat, is a dish where eggs are beaten with cheese and diced meat, then fried in rendered animal fat or meat drippings. This method gives the omelet a rich flavor and aroma typical of traditional meals popular in the late 1990s.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The dish was a common quick breakfast in cafeterias and diners during the 1990s.
Animal fat used for frying increases caloric density and enhances taste compared with vegetable oils.
Cream cheese was usually added in modest amounts so as not to overpower the meat flavor.
Typical meats included ham, bacon, or sausage pieces.
Omelets were often served with potatoes, bread, or vegetables as a side.

items.title: High-quality protein
items.content: Eggs and meat provide complete protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin source
items.content: The dish contains vitamins B2, B6, and B12, supporting energy metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Iron and zinc
items.content: Meat and eggs are good sources of iron and zinc, important for immunity and blood formation.

items.title: Calcium from cheese
items.content: Cream cheese adds calcium, contributing to bone and teeth health.

items.title: Energy-dense
items.content: Animal fat raises the calorie content, which can be beneficial for those with high energy needs.

items.title: High saturated fat
items.content: Frying in animal fat increases saturated fat intake, which may affect cholesterol levels if consumed frequently.

items.title: Caloric load
items.content: The dish is very calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable, especially on weight‑management diets.

items.title: Egg or dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to eggs or dairy proteins may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Using cured meats can add significant salt, which is a concern for people with hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the omelet hot, cut into portions. It pairs well with toast, boiled potatoes, fresh vegetables, or herbs. Optional condiments include ketchup, mustard, or a light hot sauce.

content.title: Storage
content.content: The omelet is best eaten immediately. If needed, store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Reheat gently with a little added fat to restore flavor.
